questions.title: Why was the plaintiff's request for injunctive relief rejected despite being raised in his summary judgment brief?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the court's reasoning in Section II(D). Cohen actually asked for an 'affirmative injunctive order' in his summary judgment brief. Why couldn't the court just consider that request? I thought the purpose of a summary judgment brief was to argue the merits of the claims, but the court says it wasn't 'properly' raised. Does this mean he should have filed an amended complaint specifically for the injunction?

questions.title: How does the 'legislative inaction' argument work in statutory interpretation?
questions.question_body: In Section II(A), the court denies Cohen's MPWA claim by saying that the legislature 'knew how' to grant him penalties because they did so in other sections (like § 181.13). I'm struggling to understand how a legislature's *failure* to include a specific power in one statute is used as evidence of their *intent* to exclude it. Isn't it possible they just forgot or didn't get to it yet?

questions.title: Why does a plaintiff's standing to seek civil penalties change once the underlying wages have been paid?
questions.question_body: In Section II(B), the court discusses the MFLSA claim. Cohen already received his wages and liquidated damages, but he wants the statutory penalties (which go to the government, not him). The court seems worried about 'standing.' Why does his interest in the case diminish just because the money going to *him* has been paid, if the goal of the penalty is to deter the company's ongoing behavior?

questions.title: When does a case become 'moot' if a defendant voluntarily stops a challenged practice?
questions.question_body: The court cites *Friends of the Earth* and mentions that a defendant's 'voluntary cessation' doesn't automatically strip the court of jurisdiction. However, it also says the case might be moot if it is 'absolutely clear' the behavior won't recur. As a student, I'm finding this distinction very blurry. How does a court determine what is 'absolutely clear' versus just a temporary pause by the company?

questions.title: How does the 'de novo' standard for summary judgment apply when the parties have stipulated to most of the facts?
questions.question_body: The court states it reviews the district court's summary judgment 'de novo' and must view evidence in the 'light most favorable to the nonmoving party.' However, in this case, the parties actually stipulated that Cohen was paid all wages and liquidated damages. If the facts are stipulated (agreed upon), how does the 'light most favorable' standard actually function in the court's analysis?
